KUALA LUMPUR: The judiciary will issue guidelines on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in legal proceedings within the next few weeks.

Chief Justice Tun Wan Ahmad Farid Wan Salleh said the move followed concerns over the reliability of AI-generated legal submissions, which could appear convincing despite containing inaccurate information.
"Today, AI can produce submissions that look polished and persuasive, but entirely wrong.

"On our part, we will issue a practice direction in a few weeks' time in respect of the usage of AI in legal proceedings," he said in his opening address at the International Malaysia Law Conference 2026 here yesterday.
Speaking to reporters later, Wan Ahmad Farid said the guidelines would apply to lawyers and court officers, while judges already had their own.
"We are not going to discourage them. But there has to be a guideline for them to follow."
He said AI could expedite court proceedings and save time, provided it was used responsibly.
"It is good for the speedy resolution of disputes in court. It needs to be encouraged.
"As long as it is properly used, it saves a lot of judicial time for the judges and saves time for the lawyers.
"It is something that whether we hate it or love it, it is there. So we have to embrace it," he said.
However, he cautioned against excessive reliance on AI, warning that it could undermine human reasoning and critical thinking.
In his speech, Wan Ahmad Farid said technology could speed up the workings of justice but must never replace human judgment, particularly when courts exercised judicial discretion.
"Technology can accelerate the administration of justice, but it can never become the author of justice itself.
"The duty belongs exclusively to us, human custodians of the law," he said.
He cited Malaysia's 2023 reforms abolishing the mandatory death penalty as an example of the importance of judicial discretion in ensuring fairness.
The reforms allowed judges to consider the circumstances of individual cases instead of being bound by a mandatory death sentence.

Wan Ahmad Farid said technology could not replicate the human considerations involved in administering justice, particularly when balancing the rights of accused persons with the interests of victims.
"No computer program can look into the eyes of a victim and offer vindication, nor can it look at an accused person and temper justice with mercy," he said.
He also highlighted the importance of intellectual honesty among judges and legal practitioners as technology continued to transform the profession.
Judges, he said, must ensure their judgments reflected a proper appreciation of the facts and law, including addressing arguments that challenged their conclusions.
Lawyers, meanwhile, must cite legal authorities accurately and give clients honest advice, particularly when the legal position remained uncertain.
Wan Ahmad Farid said judges must decide cases based on the law and evidence, without yielding to public pressure or external influence.
Fairness, he added, required the justice system to protect the rights of accused persons while ensuring that victims and their families were not overlooked.

b8365cf2bf687c78: In the first round of the 2026 Brazilian presidential election, on Oct. 4, the politics of resentment prevailed. Frustration among those displaced from their jobs by automation and the newly self-employed – who sometimes wrongly see themselves as “entrepreneurs” – fueled the vote for the opposition of Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and favored far right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. In the runoff on Oct. 25, however, the driving motivation shifted from resentment to fear of a return of the so-called “Bolsonarismo” to power. President Lula was reelected in a second round whose outcome could hardly have been anticipated from his lackluster first round campaign and Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead of 2.2 million votes. So what changed? First, Lula took his campaign to the streets, where it had been largely absent in the first round. And it also moved into social media, where Lula’s presence had preiviously amounted to little more than a translation of analog campaigning into digital formats. Another important factor was the fear generated by Flávio Bolsonaro’s first round lead. Until then, there had been a widespread conviction – not only among Lula and his campaign team, but throughout democratic society in general – that the president would be reelected. A change in attitudes The shock with the results of the first round, followed by fear of a far right victory, brought about a change in attitudes and a spontaneous mobilization in the streets, beginning with students in Brazil’s Rio de Janeiro state and spreading to large and medium sized cities across the country. Fear intensified as Flávio Bolsonaro increasingly revealed his resemblance to his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, now jailed for attempting a coup after losing his bid for reelection in 2022.. In the 27 state capitals and 162 other major Brazilian cities, encompassing nearly 75 million voters – close to 47% of the total – Lula’s gains were decisive, according to a survey by news and data analysis website Dado Bruto. He won in 13 of the state capitals, including São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro. In Minas Gerais, he lost in capital Belo Horizonte, although he carried the state. Overall, in the state capitals, Lula gained 2.2 million votes in the runoff, offsetting Flávio Bolsonaro’s first round advantage. Across the 189 Brazilian major cities, Lula’s vote share rose by nearly 3.5 percentage points. This result helped him make gains in every state. He reversed the first round defeat in Minas Gerais, improving his performance in the second round by more than three percentage points. Urban Brazil delivered Lula’s victory. He won in 12 states in the first round, and in 13 in the second. Consider Osasco, a major city in the state of São Paulo, whose GDP is overwhelmingly generated by the service industry, particularly finance, technology, logistics, and ecommerce. The city has nearly 729,000 inhabitants and a GDP per capita of R$ 164,000 (US$30,000). Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round in Osasco by 191,700 votes to Lula’s 182,700. In the runoff, Lula reversed the result, winning by 234,300 votes to 213,200. In many of these major cities, voters took to the streets in support of Lula. On social media, the extensive reach of the WhatsApp network “Exército do Lula” – or “Lula’s Army” –, with more than 10 million followers and managed by reelected congressman André Janones, certainly had a significant positive effect in generating additional votes for the president. The interaction between digital networks and street mobilization played a decisive, if not determining, role in his reelection. In the major cities of agribusiness strongholds, Flávio Bolsonaro won more than 70% of the runoff vote. A particularly representative municipality is Sinop, in the state of Mato Grosso, where he won the first round by 73,700 votes to Lula’s 17,500. In the runoff, Lula gained another 4,700 votes, while the Liberal Party candidate added 3,800, making little difference to the final result: 77,500 votes to 22,200, with Flávio Bolsonaro winning 77.7% of the votes. Urban-rural cleavage revived The expansion of export oriented agribusiness, particularly in Brazil’s center-west and north regions, but also in the South and the north-central and northwestern regions of Minas Gerais, has revived the urban-rural cleavage of Brazilian politics. This divide was at the heart of the most serious political and electoral conflicts of Brazil’s Second Republic, from 1945 to 1964. During that period, the troubled relationship between an executive branch elected by urban Brazil and a legislature whose majority was elected by rural Brazil produced legislative paralysis, contributing to the breakdown of democratic institutions that led to the 1964 coup. Today, although the rural economy is technologically advanced, this divide has taken the radicalized form of political polarization, destabilizing the political system and threatening the country’s governability. It generates an authoritarian impulse that materialized under Jair Bolsonaro’s administration. Jair Bolsonaro was convicted in September 2025 of attempting a coup and is serving his sentence. The prosecution and conviction of those involved in the attempted coup have dispelled neither radicalized polarization nor the authoritarian impulse. The latter resurfaced unmistakably in Flávio Bolsonaro’s refusal to accept the clean and democratic verdict of the ballot box. It was precisely this persistent coup oriented impulse that made the runoff mobilization possible, through a clearly visible interaction between digital networks and the streets. The decline in voter alienation, which brought 4.8 million electors back into the pool of valid votes, vividly expresses this reaction driven by fear of a return to Bolsonaro’s attempts to overthrow democratic institutions. Nearly 2.9 million additional voters turned out at the polls. Invalid votes fell from 3.7 million to 2.7 million, while blank ballots declined from 2.3 million to 1.4 million. Voter alienation dropped by three percentage points. The future of Lula’s fourth term This coup oriented impulse is particularly important when we consider the composition of the newly elected Brazilian Congress. A majority of those elected to Congress in the first round are sided with Flávio Bolsonaro. Beginning in 2027, President Lula’s room for maneuver in Congress will be narrower. In both the House of Deputies and the Senate, it will be possible to assemble a majority coalition, but one in which the center-right and right will carry greater weight. Members of the “Centrão”, Brazil’s parties known for their transactional politics, are inclined to align themselves with those in power by definition. 221a04c5d881621c: Maximize value, not token usage, Amazon has told its engineers, citing concerns about rising AI costs and complexity.
Amazon made the strategy shift public on Tuesday in a note to engineering teams outlining the changing role of its software development engineers in the age of AI.

“Our most prolific engineers have demonstrated that neither the developer role nor their output is defined by the use of AI,” Amazon VP and distinguished engineer Terk Terkowitz wrote in the note. “We're now in the era of the Renaissance Developer, blending AI tools with human judgment and domain expertise to build entirely new things.”
In other words, Amazon wants its developers using AI, but burning through tokens isn't the same thing as getting useful work done.
Rather than define the developer role by how AI is used, the memo focuses on what isn't changing so fast: the need to deliver useful software and results for customers and the business.

“It is difficult to define, in a way that will stand the test of time, what good AI powered engineering practices look like,” the memo continues. “We have decided to focus on what is not changing as we evolved the SDE roles … the outcomes that matter aren’t changing, even if the inputs, tools, and techniques are changing faster than ever.”

What that means for software developers in the present moment is that AI input metrics, even if Amazon has seen some correlation with increased productivity and delivery on tokenmaxxing teams, aren’t what Amazon sees as a measurement of good use of developer time and resources.
“We are all aware of how deeply flawed these metrics are, primarily because they are disconnected from what matters,” the memo argues.

“[U]sing these metrics could, if used as a target instead of a measure, drive negative outcomes, increasing costs, and increasing complexity,” the memo continues, referring to tokenmaxxing costs and overly complex code that’s at odds with Amazon’s mission to “invent and simplify.”

An Amazon spokesperson confirmed that the memo’s intent was to discourage tokenmaxxing, pointing us to comments from AWS CEO Matt Garman from June in which he encouraged developers to measure outcomes, not token consumption, in making proper use of AI tools for software development.

Amazon also wants its developers thinking more about how AI can help “improve delivery for customers” and business units, not just trying to find a place to stick it to prove it's working for them. The memo calls out some engineering teams who’ve “become less connected to their customers and business,” and says teams that are more engaged with their products and business roles “are able to take the most advantage of AI and agentic software development,” in essence calling for more teams to take a similar approach.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the memo said. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.”

Amazon's take in the memo is starkly similar to what Microsoft told its own internal development teams in August, right down to stressing a focus on returns for customers and business instead of maximizing input.
"Tokenmaxxing is not what we are optimizing for," Microsoft EVP Jay Parikh told developers. "I want all of us focused on maximizing outcomes that move the needle for our customers and our business."

With that, the writing seems to be on the wall for the throw-AI-at-everything-and-see-where-it-sticks approach to integrating the tech. When two companies that large start to question whether AI token consumption is a useful measure of productivity for their thousands of software engineers, it's possible the rest of the world will soon start sipping those tokens instead of chugging them.

That, or we'll soon see even more enterprises begin to embrace the philosophy of relying on "good enough" open-weight models that can handle many tasks at a fraction of the cost of more expensive alternatives – Garman made a similar case for choosing cost-effective models based on the task back in June.
If you're a bubble, that approach looks an awful lot like a pin. ®

6d18c5b6b9472786: MEXICO CITY: Alberto Ascari was a boyhood hero for US motor racing great Mario Andretti, now 86, but few of Kimi Antonelli's compatriots were around when Italy's last Formula One world champion was making headlines.

Antonelli, 20, is set this weekend to become the only living Italian who knows what it feels like to take the chequered flag and win the Formula One championship. He would be the first to do it in 73 years, since Ascari's second title with Ferrari in 1953.

"I know the corner in Monza is named after him," the Mercedes driver told Reuters when asked what he knew about his illustrious predecessor, who was also champion in 1952 after Giuseppe "Nino" Farina won the first title with Alfa Romeo in 1950. Farina died in 1966.
"I know that he was the last Italian champion. And it was a long time ago. A very, very long time ago."
LUCKY BLUE HELMET

Ascari was the son of a racing driver, as is Antonelli, with father Antonio a multiple race winner before his death in the 1925 French Grand Prix at Montlhery, south of Paris, long before the Formula One world championship started in 1950.
Antonio Ascari was 36 when he died, the same age almost to the day as Alberto when he crashed fatally at Monza while testing a Ferrari sportscar in 1955.
The younger Ascari had not been due to drive the car, present only to watch his friend Eugenio Castellotti in action, but decided to try it out.

Borrowing a helmet, instead of the lucky light blue one the superstitious driver always wore, and dressed in regular street clothes, the Milanese was thrown out of the car after it skidded and somersaulted off the track at the Curva del Vialone.
The chicane is now known to F1 fans as the Variante Ascari.

Four days earlier, wearing the blue helmet, he had plunged his Lancia into the Monaco harbour at the chicane coming out of the tunnel – miraculously missing an iron mooring hidden by a hay bale – and emerged relatively unscathed.
"You have to get straight back into the saddle after an accident, otherwise doubt sets in," he was quoted as telling a friend before the fateful drive.
Italians turned out in their tens of thousands for the funeral, with his blue helmet resting on the coffin, and he was buried beside his father.
"He was the fastest driver I ever saw," Britain's first world champion Mike Hawthorn recalled later. "Faster even than (Juan Manuel) Fangio."
Andretti, the 1978 world champion and now on the board of newcomers Cadillac F1, has described Ascari as his "absolute idol."
"Very cool and relaxed. He sat back doing his thing, totally in control of his car. I loved that style," the Italian-born American recalls on his website.

"When I was 14, I saw my first Formula One race in Monza, Italy — the Italian Grand Prix. Alberto Ascari didn't win that day, but he was fighting with Mercedes, the stronger team at the time," Andretti also wrote in the New York Times last April. "He was my hero regardless. That's when the dream really was cemented."
Until Antonelli came along, Ascari held the record for most wins by an Italian in a single season and for successive victories.
Ascari still holds the record for most career wins by an Italian (13 from 32 races) but, with Antonelli on nine from a single campaign, it is probably only a matter of time before that too falls.

GitHub is making more bells and whistles available through its Copilot app, including Copilot Projects, for coordinating parallel work; Copilot Connectors, for simplifying how Copilot connects to MCP servers; and Copilot Automations, which are reusable agent tasks.

AFP reporters on the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha saw one train embedded into another and some carriages lying on their side in tangles of metal debris at the bottom of an embankment.

'CHAOS'
Pablo Mejia, 42, with blood staining his grey jumper, told AFP that he had miraculously survived after changing his seat, as he awaited a transfer to the southern city of Seville.
He recounted "a very strong hit. It lasted a long time until it stopped, lots of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos."

The Renfe train restarted and travelled 25 kilometres until it collided with the stationary Iryo, at a speed that could have reached "up to 200 kilometres per hour", Puente added.
The control centre "had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it", Puente said.
RAIL SAFETY UNDER SCRUTINY

The accident comes one month before Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faced heavy criticism for this year's first disaster, seeks to overturn unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership in an early general election on November 29.

He said Spain would observe three days of mourning from Thursday, conceding it was "not acceptable" that two high-speed collisions could happen within months. His Socialists halted campaign activities.

The leader of the main opposition conservative Popular Party, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who leads in most polls, also suspended campaigning but said: "Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure."

Condolences flooded in from across Spain and Europe. The Spanish royal household said on X it was "shocked and concerned" by the accident, conveying its support to the victims, their loved ones and the emergency services.
Spain's high-speed rail network has received huge investment in recent years, growing to become the second-largest in the world after China's and a source of national pride.

But Wednesday's accident comes after another collision between two high-speed trains outside the southern village of Adamuz in January left 46 dead, which raised major questions about safety on the country's railways.
That crash was Spain's deadliest train accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela.

071e826394b5b671: For centuries, infrastructure has evolved alongside technology. New materials and engineering techniques enabled taller buildings, longer bridges, and larger cities. Computing and digital technologies later transformed how infrastructure was designed, monitored, and operated. Now, the pace of change is accelerating, and challenges are arriving simultaneously. Climate change is increasing pressure on water, energy, and other resources. Artificial intelligence is beginning to transform engineering and design, and its energy needs, along with aging grid infrastructure, is creating significant challenges, as well as new opportunities. In addition, geopolitical complexity is exposing vulnerabilities in global supply chains, and demand for infrastructure is rising, particularly in the developing world. The result is a fundamental challenge: How can the world build the infrastructure it needs without simply repeating the extractive, carbon- and resource-intensive model of the 20th century? In this interview, Ali Jadbabaie, JR East Professor and head of the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, says the answer will require rethinking not only how infrastructure is designed and built, but how it is financed and operated, and bringing together the many stakeholders who shape those decisions. On Oct. 28, Jadbabaie will join experts from around the world in Madrid to explore these topics at the World Infrastructure Forum, which was co-founded by MIT’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, UPM, the World Bank Group, and the University of Texas at Austin. Q: Infrastructure has always evolved in response to technological advances. What makes this era different? A: In the 18th century, civil engineering emerged as the civilian counterpart to military engineering, building the dams, bridges, and canals of its time. Industrialization in the 19th century brought railways and sewage systems. In the early 20th century, the focus scaled up to buildings, highways, tunnels, and metro systems, and by mid-century the infrastructure needed to support megacities and skyscrapers. Every time technology has changed, with information technologies, computing, sensing, and, more recently, digital transformation, it has changed the shape of infrastructure. It has even changed the definition of what infrastructure is. Today, we consider the power grid, semiconductor manufacturing plants, and data centers part of infrastructure, along with wireless infrastructure like cellphone towers and the infrastructure for high-speed internet, just as much a part of our critical infrastructure as roads, water systems, and power grids.  What is different now is the combination and speed of the changes we're facing. Climate change, resource constraints, and geopolitical instability are putting pressure on the way we designed infrastructure in the 20th century. At the same time, many people are moving out of poverty because of recent economic growth in the developing world. In fact, according to models, by 2028, for the first time in the history of humanity, the median human inhabitant of the planet will live off $10 a day. As more people move out of abject poverty, there will also be an increase in the demand for infrastructure. If we try to meet that demand using the same resource-intensive model we used in the 20th century, we simply won't have the resources to do it. The question then becomes: How do we use the remaining resources more efficiently? We need to find a way to provide more infrastructure while using less water, energy, and materials, and produce less carbon. This is where digital transformation and AI become potentially transformative. Faster and cheaper sensing, greater access to data, and better sensing, actuation, and control can help us make infrastructure decisions more efficiently. AI is slowly permeating the physical world, and we expect it to revolutionize the engineering design process, allowing us to explore many more possibilities, much faster and at a lower cost.  But the story of that hasn't been written yet, and the outcomes could still be very positive, depending on what we do. Q: Can you give an example of infrastructure systems becoming more interconnected in a way that changes how we build or manage them? A: The revolution in information technology and digital transformation over the past 30 years has made infrastructure systems more interconnected. You see this in cities. If the power goes out, water and gas systems can stop functioning, internet fails, and transportation system comes to a halt. If communications networks fail, many other services are affected. We saw this during Covid, when disruptions in supply chains affected energy networks, critical materials, and manufacturing. We see it when geopolitical conflicts disrupt oil and energy markets and those disruptions propagate through other parts of the global economy. Infrastructure systems that were once managed separately are increasingly dependent on one another. As we connect more things together for more efficiency, we also increase systemic risk and expose the systems to rare but catastrophic failures. They have become rare, but when they happen, they're much bigger and more consequential. The really tricky thing is that developing infrastructure involves much more than designing and building it. The whole value chain includes financing and operating it, as well as understanding who will use it and what those users need and prefer. So, designing infrastructure is a highly transdisciplinary, sociotechnical endeavor, involving social, technical, and economic considerations. Understanding how these systems are designed is increasingly important because they are becoming more complex, making decision-making particularly difficult. There’s also so much uncertainty in large infrastructure projects. They’re very capital-intensive, the business is lower margin than many other industries, and projects take a long time. Combine all of that, and it has historically made the industry very conservative. But the transformations coming from AI and digital transformation are potentially offering a new way forward. What that new way looks like, no one has quite delineated it yet. Q: How are you and your colleagues working to change how these decisions get made?   A: We realized that if we're going to develop a new approach to infrastructure, no single discipline, company, or country can do it alone. Infrastructure value chain is too interconnected, and the challenges are too large. That's why MIT’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering co-founded the World Infrastructure Forum with the World Bank Group, the Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, and University of Texas at Austin. The goal is to bring together academia, industry, governments, and financial institutions across the infrastructure value chain and create an ongoing dialogue about how infrastructure should be designed, financed, built, and operated in the decades ahead. This is particularly important because the biggest opportunities for new infrastructure development are not necessarily in the United States or other countries with mature infrastructure systems. Those countries still face significant needs for modernization and new investment. But over the coming decades, much of the world's population growth, and much of the infrastructure that will need to be built, will be in countries where infrastructure systems are still developing.  Those countries have an opportunity to benefit from modern infrastructure without simply repeating the model of the 20th century. But capturing that opportunity will require new approaches to technology, financing, engineering, and governance. We're trying to create an ecosystem rather than just a forum, a mechanism for continuing the conversation among the different stakeholders across the infrastructure value chain. We've established five working groups and an advisory group of more than 30 leaders from across the infrastructure value chain, including engineering and construction, materials, finance, multilateral institutions, and academia. Ultimately, the question is not whether we need a new way of developing infrastructure. The question is how we create it and who is going to execute it. There is no single person, company, or country that can solve this problem, because infrastructure itself is interconnected. We need to build the new model together.

cdc4c7ebb97a6830: UNITED States President Donald Trump's strategy for the midterm elections has one main ingredient — more Donald Trump. But his historic unpopularity may hinder Republicans instead of helping them.

Trump has blitzed the campaign trail in the month before the Nov 3 vote, jetting across the country for near-daily rallies in the fervent belief that he alone can fire up his "Make America Great Again" base.
Add a sprinkle of insults painting Democrats as communists or fans of "transgender mutilation", add some promises of cash if Republicans win, and you have Trump's recipe for defying the polls.

"Trump believes that he is the answer to all the Republicans' woes, and is rushing to tell everyone who will listen," Peter Loge, director of George Washington University's School of Media and Public Affairs, said.
At a rare Republican Party midterms convention in Dallas in September, Trump admitted as much.
"Pretend I'm on the ballot, just one more time," the second-term president said.
By turning the 2028 midterms into a referendum on his presidency, Trump is counting on his own history of political upsets, from his shock 2016 election win to the 2024 comeback.
The problem this time is that Trump's own approval rating has hit record lows in recent polls, and is the lowest for any president heading into midterm elections since 1946.

"On balance Trump's presence in campaigns will probably hurt Republicans — partly because the president's party always does badly in the midterms, but also because he's historically unpopular," said Loge.
Trump may get his base to the polls, but there are "not enough of those dedicated Trump voters to make a difference".
With Republicans fearing they could lose control of both the House and the Senate in a Democratic "blue wave", there have been increasing signs of desperation.
Trump has changed his plans to repeatedly rally in states that once seemed solidly Republican red, particularly Texas. And he says he expects to spend US$400 million in campaign cash on the midterms.
The desperation has spilled into Trump's rhetoric.
As the campaign has worn on, Trump has peppered his freewheeling rallies with ever more polarising and violent language.

He has branded Abdul El-Sayed, the Muslim, left-wing Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, a "jihadist", used anti-trans slurs against another Democrat, called Democrats communists and stepped up his diatribes against the media.
That's when he's not veering off into bizarre tangents.
In recent days, for example, he has obsessed about both men's and women's behinds, from Ohio Senator Jon Husted to rapper Nicki Minaj.
But while die-hard supporters may cheer Trump's raucous speeches, ordinary Republicans may be turned off. And even if they can't stomach switching to Democrats, they may simply stay at home.
Trump's other strategy is to throw money at the problem — but only if Republicans win.

He has promised a US$5,000 dividend for every adult American if Republicans keep control of Congress — despite questions about whether it would be legal and how he would fund the US$1 trillion cost. Yet polls show most Americans doubt that they will ever get the US$5,000 payments.
Trump is also offering goodies for voters hit by high fuel costs from the Iran war, including bailouts for farmers and easing sanctions on Canada to help border towns.
But Trump's efforts to bring down oil costs have had mixed results.
His Iran war has stalled, but he is widely reported to be considering fresh strikes with Israel after the midterms.
A diesel deal with Russia has meanwhile sparked accusations that Trump is selling out Ukraine.
Trump's most important midterms strategy may be what he does afterwards.
Questions are already mounting about whether he will challenge a midterms loss like he did in the 2020 presidential election.

Trump on Monday announced US$1 million rewards for information leading to vote fraud convictions, and last week he ordered a preemptive suit to block the Alaska Senate result if the Republican incumbent loses.
"I'm sceptical that Trump will go quiet into that good night," said Loge.

616ede8369b17264: MEXICO CITY: Alberto Ascari was a boyhood hero for US motor racing great Mario Andretti, now 86, but few of Kimi Antonelli's compatriots were around when Italy's last Formula One world champion was making headlines.
Antonelli, 20, is set this weekend to become the only living Italian who knows what it feels like to take the chequered flag and win the Formula One championship.
He would be the first to do it in 73 years, since Ascari's second title with Ferrari in 1953.

"I know the corner in Monza is named after him," the Mercedes driver told Reuters when asked what he knew about his illustrious predecessor, who was also champion in 1952 after Giuseppe "Nino" Farina won the first title with Alfa Romeo in 1950. Farina died in 1966.
"I know that he was the last Italian champion. And it was a long time ago. A very, very long time ago," he said.
Lucky blue helmet

Ascari was the son of a racing driver, as is Antonelli, with father Antonio a multiple race winner before his death in the 1925 French Grand Prix at Montlhery, south of Paris, long before the Formula One world championship started in 1950.
Antonio Ascari was 36 when he died, the same age almost to the day as Alberto when he crashed fatally at Monza while testing a Ferrari sportscar in 1955.
The younger Ascari had not been due to drive the car, present only to watch his friend Eugenio Castellotti in action, but decided to try it out.

Borrowing a helmet, instead of the lucky light blue one the superstitious driver always wore, and dressed in regular street clothes, the Milanese was thrown out of the car after it skidded and somersaulted off the track at the Curva del Vialone.
The chicane is now known to F1 fans as the Variante Ascari.

Four days earlier, wearing the blue helmet, he had plunged his Lancia into the Monaco harbour at the chicane coming out of the tunnel - miraculously missing an iron mooring hidden by a hay bale - and emerged relatively unscathed.
"You have to get straight back into the saddle after an accident, otherwise doubt sets in," he was quoted as telling a friend before the fateful drive.
Italians turned out in their tens of thousands for the funeral, with his blue helmet resting on the coffin, and he was buried beside his father.
"He was the fastest driver I ever saw," Britain's first world champion Mike Hawthorn recalled later. "Faster even than (Juan Manuel) Fangio".
Andretti, the 1978 world champion and now on the board of newcomers Cadillac F1, has described Ascari as his "absolute idol".
"Very cool and relaxed. He sat back doing his thing, totally in control of his car. I loved that style," the Italian-born American recalls on his website.

"When I was 14, I saw my first Formula One race in Monza, Italy — the Italian Grand Prix. Alberto Ascari didn’t win that day, but he was fighting with Mercedes, the stronger team at the time," Andretti also wrote in the New York Times last April. "He was my hero regardless. That’s when the dream really was cemented," he said.
Until Antonelli came along, Ascari held the record for most wins by an Italian in a single season and for successive victories.
Ascari still holds the record for most career wins by an Italian (13 from 32 races) but, with Antonelli on nine from a single campaign, it is probably only a matter of time before that too falls.
ee0f6bebf043544c: Ukrainian ransomware crook Artem Stryzhak has been sentenced to 70 months in the slammer by a New York federal court for his role as an affiliate of the Nefilim and Hive ransomware gangs.
Prosecutors believe the cybercriminal began working with Nefilim in or around June 2021, while living in Barcelona, Spain.

The Nefilim ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was known for targeting wealthy companies, with its operators encouraging affiliates to pursue businesses capable of paying substantial ransom demands.
One of Nefilim's most high-profile attacks was on Australian logistics giant Toll Group in 2020, encrypting its files roughly three months after it suffered a separate Mailto ransomware attack.
Court documents [PDF] state that Stryzhak agreed with alleged Nefilim boss Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, who remains at large, to pay the ransomware crew a 20 percent cut of the ransom proceeds he collected.

Tymoshchuk told Stryzhak that his preference was for attacks to target companies based in the US, Canada, and Australia that turn over more than $100 million annually. This guidance was soon tweaked to encourage targeting companies in the same regions with more than $200 million in annual revenue.

Prosecutors claim that around the time Stryzhak joined forces with Nefilim, he also signed up to the Hive ransomware operation as "one of its earliest affiliates," and used its platform to attack approximately seven victims. Hive's operators claimed they targeted circa 1,500 victims worldwide between June 2021 and January 2023.

According to separate court documents [PDF], Hive's victims included a law firm and an Ohio hospital, which paid approximately $1.7 million in Bitcoin after the gang initially demanded $2 million during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Before its infrastructure was seized in an international law enforcement operation in January 2023, Hive was known for attacking healthcare facilities during the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as being one of the ransomware groups that battered Costa Rica in 2022.

Brett Leatherman, assistant director at the FBI’s cyber branch, described Stryzhak as a “prolific cybercriminal” who played a role in groups that were responsible for more than $100 million in victim damages.
“Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners,” he said.

“Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.”
Stryzhak was arrested by Spanish police in June 2024 before being extradited to the US in April 2025.

In announcing Stryzhak's sentencing, the Justice Department took the opportunity to remind the public that rewards totaling up to $11 million are available for qualifying information about alleged Nefilim operator Volodymyr Tymoshchuk and other key ransomware suspects. ®
9d3ee357777bb88b: KUALA LUMPUR: Kementerian Kewangan (MoF) memaklumkan Suruhanjaya Pencegahan Rasuah Malaysia (SPRM) masih menjalankan proses siasatan terhadap pelaburan Kumpulan Wang Persaraan (Diperbadankan) (KWAP) dalam syarikat teknologi akuakultur Indonesia, eFishery.

Kenyataan itu menjawab pertanyaan Kalam Salan (PN-Sabak Bernama) yang meminta kerajaan mengesahkan pelaburan KWAP kira-kira RM200 juta dalam eFishery yang terdedah kepada penipuan.

Menurut MoF, pelaburan dalam eFishery telah melalui proses penilaian dan tadbir urus yang ditetapkan termasuk pengesahan juruaudit antarabangsa bertauliah berdasarkan maklumat yang tersedia ketika itu.

Bagaimanapun, menurutnya, syarikat berkenaan kemudiannya didapati terlibat dalam manipulasi kewangan yang disengajakan serta penyelewengan fakta dalam laporan kewangan syarikat. "Keadaan ini berlaku walaupun proses penilaian yang dilaksanakan telah merangkumi penilaian dalaman, usaha wajar bebas serta penelitian terhadap aspek kewangan, perundangan dan operasi sebelum cadangan pelaburan diluluskan.
"Malah, beberapa pelabur institusi global utama turut terjejas akibat salah laku berkenaan," menurutnya.

MoF memaklumkan KWAP merupakan pemegang saham minoriti dalam eFishery manakala sebahagian besar saham syarikat tersebut dipegang oleh pelabur lain termasuk pelabur institusi global utama.

4b656c9c0a9c825f: KING Charles III began a Caribbean tour in the Bahamas on Tuesday where he acknowledged "the great suffering of the past" in the face of pressure to apologise for the slave trade.
The 77-year-old king, who is receiving treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer, will also highlight climate threats facing low-lying islands during the visit to three countries in nine days.

He will first make solo visits to the Bahamas and Guyana, before being joined by his wife, Queen Camilla, for the final leg in Antigua and Barbuda, where he will address a Commonwealth Heads of Government (CHOGM) summit.
"We know that some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness," he said at a youth rally.

"It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future."

He said leaders of "affected" Commonwealth nations would be discussing the issue in Antigua and Barbuda next week where the issue of reparations for slavery will be on the table according to Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey.
Several of the former colonies have demanded the king take a new step towards making amends for colonisation and the transatlantic slave trade, from which his ancestors profited for centuries.
As he arrived at the rally held at the historic site where the Bahamas officially gained its independence in 1973, protesters gathered to wave placards reading "pay what you owe us."

Last month Jamaica — where Charles remains head of state — filed a petition in an appeals court in London "to advance Jamaica's push for reparations for the African ancestors who suffered under hundreds of years of enslavement".
Charles has previously called slavery the "darkest days" of British history, and will address colonial issues at each stage of the trip.
Few in royal circles will have forgotten a turbulent 2022 trip to Jamaica by Prince William, when he and Princess Catherine were met with anti-monarchy protests and calls for reparations.
Guyana's President Irfaan Ali, who is to meet with Charles during the visit, told ITV News the king's recognition of the "darkest days" was just the "first step".
"Now, moving to the apology is the next step," said Ali, demanding accountability from the former empire which he said "exploited the region", "destroyed lives" and "created under development".

Modern monarchs have to various degrees expressed remorse for Britain's central role in chattel slavery, but none has yet formally apologised. The debt-laden United Kingdom government has balked at the idea of financial compensation.
Botchwey told Sky News ahead of the government meeting from Nov 1 to 4, that it "wouldn't hurt" for the king to apologise.
Botchwey also said the "time has come" to discuss reparations, in the form of financial payments or otherwise.
Buckingham Palace has insisted the tour is an opportunity for the king to look forward, meet young people and discuss pressing issues like climate change.
In his Bahamas speech, Charles also highlighted the particular threat facing low-lying islands face from climate change.

"In an island nation where 90 per cent of the land sits below two meters. There is perhaps nowhere better than the Bahamas to understand the reality of climate change that threatens so many communities across the Commonwealth," he said.
"Our world cries out for healing."
According to Botchwey, the Commonwealth, which includes 56 member countries with the king at its helm, is an important anchor in a "world that is almost spinning out of control".
"This CHOGM is going to be one like never before," the secretary-general said in an interview, with the meeting in St John's set to focus on investment and trade opportunities for member countries.

623841ef72de0a54: THE reason why migrant workers, refugees and asylum seekers desperately enter Malaysia by any means necessary is also why they attract human smugglers.
Human trafficking is a burgeoning business because of Malaysia's strategic location, reliance on migrant labour and vulnerabilities in law enforcement and border control.

In one clean sweep, Malaysia is a lucrative source, transit hub and destination country for criminal syndicates. The coastline, including the Strait of Malacca, is riddled with smuggling entry points while the dense forest shared with Thailand is ideal cover for refugees and migrants from Myanmar and Bangladesh to enter Perlis, Kedah, Perak and Kelantan.
Because of stringent labour policies and expensive work permits, labourers and employers sidestep legal immigration red tape, fuelling the black market for smuggling operations.

The United States Department of State's Trafficking in Persons Report designated Malaysia at Tier 2, which meant that Malaysia has yet to meet minimum international standards to eliminate human trafficking.

Border control is managed by dedicated enforcement officers, unsung heroes whose feats are barely understood by the general public. But a tragedy highlighted just how crucial their jobs are: on Oct 27, Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency sailor Mohd Roshaimi Mohd Ridzuan was killed and three colleagues injured while pursuing a boat carrying illegal migrants.

Their patrol boat collided with a coastal seawall at Sungai Padang during a high-speed pursuit. There were previous incidents: last year, a boat carrying illegal immigrants off Tanjung Kling rammed into an enforcement patrol boat, injuring two MMEA officers.

The incidents reflect the volatile and dangerous night surveillance and sea chases against heavily armed rogue operators. That's not all: MMEA officers have survived machete attacks. Roshaimi's tragic death in the line of duty must strengthen, not weaken, Malaysia's resolve to dismantle these smuggling syndicates.

While we pay tribute to the fallen sailor, we must acknowledge the risks faced by the MMEA. The best tribute we could offer is the funds and resources for a better-prepared, better-equipped and intelligence-led enforcement.

In the meantime, we must remove and indict compromised border control officers through continuous spot checks at border checkpoints and visa-processing agencies. Make it mandatory for employer-pays mechanisms to prevent migrant workers' accruing massive debts to third-party agents.

Businesses using unauthorised sub-contractors or ignore illegal workforce must be subjected to punitive penalties. Deploy drone patrols, thermal imaging and biometric tracking and train enforcement officers to distinguish deliberate illegal immigrants from coerced or deceived victims.
133598f3f99fbe16: Donate to our Justice as infrastructure Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!

All images via Canva or fair use. Screenshots of Peacekeeping circle (bottom left) and Duterte protest (top center) via YouTube. International Criminal Court building (top right) via Wikimedia CC BY-SA 4.0. St. Louis courthouse under construction (center middle) via Picryl CC0 1.0.

Often portrayed as abstract, large, formal, distant, and quite technical, justice is a moral and ethical area, tied to institutions and legal statutes, and can seem a long way from mundane daily experience. But it is also a deeply practical underpinning for how most societies function. Without justice systems that work and are understood at the most fundamental level, economic mobility is threatened, socially marginalized groups have no recourse, and lack of trust hampers institutions and interpersonal interactions alike.

Justice is the grease in the motor of social functioning. Nobody will contest the importance of justice to holding people to a collective moral code of conduct, but the often overlooked next-level function justice plays is that, when justice is fair, fast, and reliable, it makes everything in a society run better. It allows for a society to fulfill its economic, social, and creative potential. Copyright law protects ideas and innovation; land law protects resources and livelihoods; labor law supports humane and effective use of our work — as long as those laws are enforced. When you know that it will be straightforward and predictable to get all the permits, you are more likely to start a business. When you know that fraud will be punished, you are more likely to invest your capital. When you know that you will be caught, you’re less likely to evade taxes. When you know that there will be fair and fast prosecution, you are more likely to report injustice and less likely to perpetrate it.

In this spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to make visible the ways in which justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society, and how countries with a justice deficit can work towards stronger protections that will enable economic and social benefits.

f2369deb6850e771: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysian creators must understand that copyright protects original work expressed in material form, not ideas alone, an intellectual property lawyer said.

Speaking on Beyond the Headlines in conjunction with World Animation Day, Mahendra Balakrishnan said original work must be expressed in a tangible form, such as a drawing, script, photograph or film, to qualify for copyright protection.
He advised creators to keep records of their work, store files securely and limit the sharing of concepts and designs before taking steps to protect them.
He also urged creators to understand their contractual rights, particularly the distinction between licensing and assigning copyright, before allowing others to use their work.
"Always put it down on paper or put it down on a sketch, put it down on a dated document with a time stamp where possible," he said.
Licensing allows another party to use the work under agreed terms, while assignment transfers the copyright or rights specified in the agreement, Mahendra said.
He urged creators to be aware of unauthorised commercial use of their work, including reproductions and adaptations of existing characters or designs.

On generative artificial intelligence (AI), Mahendra said Malaysia's copyright framework was human-centric, with authorship and human contribution remaining important considerations in determining intellectual property rights.
He said proposed amendments to the Copyright Act 1987 were expected to address emerging issues, including generative AI.

Meanwhile, WAU Animation co-founder and Agent Ali creator Muhammad Usama Zaid said building a successful animation property involved more than producing a series or film, as its characters and stories could be extended into merchandise and other commercial ventures.
"The idea is always to tell the right story, create the right character, and then once you have the visibility, we can extend from there," he said.
Usama said he had initially aspired to work for internationally renowned animation studios such as Pixar, Disney or DreamWorks while studying animation.
However, an opportunity to develop a local animated feature redirected his focus towards building Malaysia's animation industry.
Less than a year after graduating, he and several friends had the opportunity to establish a studio and work on Geng: Pengembaraan Bermula, which he described as a catalyst for Upin & Ipin.
His experience in the industry also influenced his approach to developing Agent Ali, with the team recognising the potential for an animated property to expand beyond television and film.

Usama said the studio had to tackle the unauthorised distribution of Agent Ali The Movie 2, including recordings made in cinemas that were later shared on Telegram or edited into shorter clips for TikTok.
He said the studio worked with fans to identify the material before its digital team pursued takedowns.
Unauthorised merchandise was another concern, particularly when sellers downloaded existing images of Agent Ali characters and reproduced them on clothing, bags and other products for sale.

Usama distinguished such commercial activity from fan art, in which artists create their own interpretations of the characters. While fan art could reflect appreciation for the property, selling products featuring copied images could generate revenue without the studio's authorisation, he said.
On AI, Usama said his concerns extended beyond copyright infringement to the technology's potential impact on the creative process.
He said relying on AI without developing the underlying skills could deprive people of opportunities to learn through experimentation, problem-solving and refining their work.
Usama also cautioned creators against becoming so protective of their ideas that they avoided seeking feedback.
When developing Agent Ali, the team built a circle of trusted people who could offer candid feedback and identify weaknesses in the work, he said.
He added that the series had undergone numerous revisions, feedback sessions and brainstorming exercises before its first episode was released.
"Don't create in a silo," he said.
Usama said young artists should be valued for their work even before their creations became commercially successful, adding that creative disciplines were often treated as secondary to other fields.
World Animation Day is observed annually on Oct 28.

2a665cba9f8ba4af: PETALING JAYA: Seeking full autonomy over education would be too costly for Sarawak, says the state's education, innovation and talent development minister Roland Sagah Wee Inn.
Sagah said teachers' salaries alone would cost the state a significant amount every year, Borneo Post reported.

“We cannot afford to spend that amount of money. Imagine how many teachers and schools there are. If we are going to spend it, we might as well put it toward other developments instead," he was quoted as saying after officiating the 4th International Conference on Educational Research and Innovation 2026 in Kuching today.
At the same time, he said, major federal taxes are taken by the central government.
Sagah said major administrative issues between the state government and the education ministry had been resolved.
He said Sarawak's priority was to ensure greater flexibility in managing education matters.
“Don't misunderstand the meaning of autonomy. As long as there is ease of doing business, that is enough for us,” he said.

He cited the agreement allowing English to be used to teach Mathematics and Science, as well as the Sarawak Dual Language Programme Assessment Test (UP-DLP) as examples of progress in the state's education autonomy.
Sagah also said Sarawak was incorporating artificial intelligence and digitalisation into the syllabuses of all teacher training institutes to help educators use the technology in their work.
He said the state was still behind developed countries in this area, but was catching up.
33c673a8d5cb4cdb: A cartoon from an ex-Google software engineer, titled “Welcome to Google,” made the rounds a while back. It featured two diverging roads, neither passable. One was the main road, marked as deprecated (“don’t even think about it,” the sign read). The new road, however, was marked as still under construction (“Danger”), and so was unusable as well.

That was the no-win choice two million frontend developers faced in 2014, when Google unexpectedly deprecated its popular JavaScript framework, AngularJS, in favor of Angular 2, which had a radically different architecture, a confusing name, no upgrade path, and wasn’t even fully released yet.
So, many developers turned the wheel and headed to Reactville or Vuetown instead.

How Google botched the Angular upgrade provides timely lessons in how not to update a software package, which former Google Developer Advocate Stephen Fluin outlined in a talk at the All Things Open conference last week.
“Uncertainty kills motivation,” said Fluin. “When you're taking away everything [developers] know and love, they're going to feel disheartened.”
Fluin is now head of developer relations for Buildkite, but he worked for Google from 2016 to 2021 on the Angular project.

“Things were a little bit rough at the time. It was a bit of a death march,” he told the audience. “We had no idea when Angular 2 was going to come out, and the core fundamentals of Angular kept changing.”
From AngularJS to Angular 2
Google had good reasons for updating Angular.

The AngularJS team had been snatched from Google’s infrastructure division and placed under its ad division, where the software could be more fully exploited. To support operations of that size, Angular needed greater rigor.

The original AngularJS was launched in 2009 as a side project of Google engineer Miško Hevery, who wanted to extend HTML. Google pulled AngularJS into an internal project because Google developers found it easier to work with than the Java-based Google Web Toolkit (GWT).
The framework quickly caught on with outside web developers too, who readily understood the angle brackets of HTML (hence the name) and wanted more interactive components.
Hevery built AngularJS 1.3 with a traditional controller model, which handled all user input, logic and data transport under the JavaScript $scope object.

Angular 2, announced at the ng-europe 2014 conference, was a major shift in architecture. It shifted to a component model, with each HTML template enjoying its own class properties. After a forced, unhappy dalliance with Google's Dart, the team rewrote Angular completely in TypeScript, with no backward compatibility whatsoever.

It was a lot to take in, and the introductory talk at ng-europe seemed to spook Angular developers more than inspire them. For each discarded feature, the speakers displayed a graphic of a tombstone (“RIP Controllers”) and played a recording of a church bell tolling in the background.
“That talk is still infamous today for what it did to the community,” Fluin said. “All these things that you know and love about AngularJS are gone. They're dead. And nobody knew this was coming.”

In general, it was not a good time for software migrations, Fluin noted in his talk. Python was having a rough time migrating from version 2 to 3, as was the KDE desktop moving from version 4 to version 5. And the rocky transition from GNOME 2 to 3 still loomed in the rearview mirror for many.
What's in a name?
“If you're trying to bring your developers with you, give them a path. Don't just kill your old thing and then not have a new thing ready,” Fluin advised.
Many devs defected to React and Vue.js, two other JavaScript frontend frameworks that also embraced the component model and were already in production.

In the 2016 State of JS Survey, React was the most popular frontend framework, with 53 percent of JS devs reporting that they had used it. Angular’s audience was heavily bifurcated; 30 percent still used the classic version while only 13 percent used Angular 2. Ten percent of users adopted the still up-and-coming Vue.

Angular 2 was finally released in September 2016, followed by Angular 4 the following March. Version 3 was skipped entirely for no discernable reason. Meanwhile, AngularJS classic, which was not formally retired until the end of 2021, was updated to version 1.5 in the spring of 2016, introducing components.

Muddying the waters further was the naming of the frameworks, which confounded many casual observers. Was AngularJS different from Angular 2? And was the “2” part of the Angular name, signaling the complete architectural shift, or its version number?

Getting the public to understand the name change turned out to be a major quagmire. Fluin said: “We had to fix public communication guidelines. We had to train experts. We had to fix Google's knowledge graph,” which is Google’s database of facts about the world.
“Naming and versioning matter,” he told the audience. “They don't matter in a pure technical sense, but they matter to human beings because it's human beings you're trying to keep up to date with.”

It would be easy to blame the Google brass for nearly shipwrecking Angular, but it has been a success at meeting Google’s needs. Today, the component-driven Angular powers Gemini’s user interface, Google Analytics, and countless other Google apps. It is now converging with Google’s internal Wiz high-performance framework, originally designed for the ill-fated Google+ social network.

Angular has also settled into a more predictable and user-friendly update pattern. Updates have a routine release cadence, currently twice a year. They dutifully follow semantic versioning guidelines, with major version numbers signifying breaking changes. Google tests each new version of the framework on its own apps before releasing it publicly. Any feature slated for removal is deprecated for a year first.
But in retrospect, Google may have been better off giving Angular 2 an entirely different name, even if it meant building up a new user base from scratch.
“JavaScript developers loved trying new frameworks. So, pretending to be a new framework might have been better,” Fluin told The Register. ®
73fb413e96278cc7: KUANTAN: A foreigner was arrested for allegedly injuring an auxiliary policeman and damaging casino equipment at Sky Casino in Genting Highlands yesterday.

Acting Bentong police chief Deputy Superintendent Azmi Mahmod said preliminary investigations revealed that the 34-year-old man, believed to have been drunk, had behaved aggressively towards members of the public before entering the casino.
He said the man then damaged the screens of three gambling machines by repeatedly banging his head against them, as well as two chairs, resulting in estimated losses of RM85,000.
"The man sustained a forehead injury that required six stitches," he said in a statement.
Azmi said the man also allegedly punched a 32-year-old auxiliary policeman in the mouth, breaking two of his teeth.
He said the policeman had since received treatment at Bentong Hospital.
Initial checks revealed that the man had no criminal record, he said, adding that the foreigner tested negative for drugs.
The case is being investigated under Sections 323 and 427 of the Penal Code for voluntarily causing hurt and committing mischief resulting in property damage, respectively.
The first carries a jail term of up to a year, or a fine or both upon conviction, while the second can lead to between one and five years' jail or fine, or both.
3360414e7973bd38: LONDON: Britain's economy will grow slightly faster than forecast this year before slowing in 2027, finance minister John Healey said Wednesday as he delivered the government's annual budget.
"War in the Middle East is a key driver affecting" these forecasts, Healey told parliament.
Gross domestic product (GDP) is estimated to grow by 1.2% in 2026, Healey said, up from a government estimate of 1.1% given shortly after the start of the US-Iran war.
The minister added GDP growth would slow to 1.0% next year after Labour had forecast a 2027 expansion of 1.6% in early March.
The government relies on the Office for Budget Responsibility, an independent fiscal watchdog, for its estimates.
The International Monetary Fund earlier this month also upgraded its 2026 forecast for UK GDP while downgrading its outlook for next year.
It comes after Britain's economy grew more than initially estimated in the second quarter, by 0.5%, according to official data.
The Bank of England will update its own forecasts for the UK economy on Nov 5, alongside an expected hike to its benchmark interest rate as inflation stays high.

47d2587ed91806bc: AI tools are making it easier to modify and recreate games, raising questions about piracy, copyright and how far the technology could disrupt the industry • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here If your social media algorithms have clocked that you’re into video games, something strange will have happened in the past few weeks. Your feed, like mine, will have been full of clips of streamers playing bizarre mashups of popular video games. Skyrim in Minecraft. Halo, except the main character is Mario. Skate 2 in Call of Duty maps. A flood of professional-looking fan-coded game mods that are mildly interesting to look at for 30 seconds, but ultimately inconsequential. Would I download a mod that lets me play Wii Bowling inside a zombie shooter? No, but I am very interested in where they came from. Of course, the answer – or at least, most of the answer – is AI. After a week of researching this (thanks especially to Replay Mode on YouTube for this informative video, which set me down this track) I now understand that these mashup mods are not just AI-generated videos, but AI-assisted coding. Basically, as of a few weeks ago, Anthropic’s Claude has become extremely good at decompiling video game code. Games are written by humans in readable code and then compiled into binary 1s and 0s that the PC or console running it can read; decompiling is the reversal of that process, revealing a game’s source code, which humans can then edit and mess around with for fun. This used to be an extremely laborious process. But now it is not, because humans aren’t doing much of it any more. Continue reading...

e490d7d662cabb19: KUALA LUMPUR: Barisan Nasional and its strategic partner Pas, representing parties under Perikatan Nasional, today formalised their cooperation and political understanding ahead of the 16th Melaka election.

Umno secretary-general Datuk Dr Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki said the memorandum of understanding (MoU) was signed this evening by him and PN secretary-general Datuk Seri Takiyuddin Hassan, who is also Pas secretary-general.
BN chairman Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi witnessed the signing.

"The Umno Supreme Council, which met today, unanimously agreed to formalise cooperation and a political understanding with strategic partners Pas and other parties under PN to face the Melaka election," he told reporters after the council meeting at Menara Dato Onn.

Asyraf said the supreme council had also agreed that BN and PN would launch a joint election manifesto, pledging to provide the best services to the people and build on the achievements in public service delivery and state development under the previous Melaka state government.
"The manifesto will be launched in the evening after nomination day (on Saturday). If there are any changes, we will inform later," he said.
He added that the party's election machinery and supporters would be directed to assist and provide strong support to all PN candidates contesting in the election.

"The supreme council also called on party leaders and election machinery to conduct their campaigns prudently and ethically, without resorting to slander, ridicule or insults against opposing parties," he said.
Asked whether Parti Wawasan would also field their candidates, Asyraf said the matter should be referred to PN.

"That is for PN to decide. We leave it to them to determine the candidates and the parties that will contest the seven state seats, as agreed upon under the terms of the agreement and understanding reached with BN.
"BN will contest 21 seats, including two allocated to MCA and one to MIC, while PN will contest seven seats," he said.

Meanwhile, BN Melaka chairman and caretaker Chief Minister Datuk Seri Ab Rauf Yusoh said the meeting discussed the coordination of campaign activities for the state election, with clear instructions for everyone to focus on the 21 constituencies being contested.
"Every vote counts in our efforts to defend all 21 constituencies," he said.
The Election Commission has set polling day for Nov 14, with early voting on Nov 10.
In the 2021 Melaka election, BN won 21 of the 28 seats contested, enabling it to form the state government. Pakatan Harapan won five seats, while PN secured two.
f945cf98ce47877f: URDA: A high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed 64 people and injured scores more on Wednesday, with the toll likely to rise, authorities said in one of Europe's deadliest such disasters this century.
AFP reporters on the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha saw one train embedded into another after the second such accident to strike Spain this year.
Some carriages were lying on their side in tangles of metal debris at the bottom of an embankment, while dozens of emergency services vehicles were racing to and from the site.

"We are speaking of approximately 64 (dead), but this is probably going to grow even more," Castilla-La Mancha's leader Emiliano Garcia-Page told reporters at the scene, raising a previous toll of 31.
A spokeswoman from the Castilla-La Mancha government told AFP that more than 100 people had been injured. Of them, 58 had been taken to hospital, with 15 in a critical condition.
Helicopters hovered above the site during a frantic search for survivors, while several black vans arrived from a funeral parlour.

State railway operator Renfe confirmed in a statement that the main high-speed line from Madrid to southern Spain had been suspended after one of its services suffered an accident with a train from private Spanish company Iryo.
Iryo said in a statement that its train, which was carrying 147 passengers and five staff including the driver, "was hit from behind" by the Renfe service.
A visibly shaken Manuel Ortiz, 49, who lives in the nearby village of Urda, around 130km south of Madrid, told AFP he had been transporting survivors all morning in his car.
Ortiz added that the passengers of the Iryo told him their train was stationary when the collision happened, describing a "horrific, horrible" scene that "smelled of an accident, of metal".
Rail safety under scrutiny

The accident comes one month before Socialist prime minister Pedro Sanchez, who faced heavy criticism for this year's first disaster, seeks to overturn unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership in an early general election on Nov 29.
Sanchez's office said he was heading to the scene. The premier had said on X that he was "shocked" by the accident and sent "my love, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families".

Condolences flooded in from across Spain and Europe. The Spanish royal household said on X it was "shocked and concerned" by the accident, conveying its support to the victims, their loved ones and the emergency services.
An EU spokeswoman said the bloc was "ready to help Spain if needed", while European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said "Europe mourns" with the victims after the "devastating news".
The Spanish football federation postponed 24 matches in the first round of the Copa del Rey "as a mark of respect and solidarity".
Spain's high-speed rail network has received huge investment in recent years, growing to become the world's second-largest after China and a source of national pride.

However, Wednesday's accident comes after another collision between two high-speed trains outside the southern village of Adamuz in January left 46 dead, which raised major questions about safety on the country's railways.
That crash was Spain's deadliest train accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela.
Both of this year's accidents happened on the line linking Madrid to the southern city of Seville.

The cause of the latest disaster, which happened on a straight stretch of track in sunny, dry conditions, was unknown. Five people wearing white overalls were examining the tracks and taking photographs, AFP saw.
One of the country's busiest routes, it was Spain's first high-speed line when it opened in 1992 to coincide with the Seville universal exposition.
fdc9c053616efe5d: You've probably heard, at this point, about the big changes coming to Meta's AI scraping terms for business accounts. Nieman Lab had that scoop, and since then, small businesses, journalists, and artists using Meta products like Instagram have been raising the alarm. But if you're in the EU or UK, you might be in luck and can object to that use of your data, as some users have pointed out.
If You're In the UK or EU, Here's How to Object to Meta's AI Training

Earlier this month, Meta updated its commercial terms of use for business accounts to allow it to “use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta’s products.

Many artists and small business owners that rely on Instagram and Facebook are livid at Meta granting itself permission to use their content, including from websites simply connected to their Meta accounts, to train AI. But for users in the United Kingdom and European Union, for now, there’s a way to object.

Meta buried this change in its Commercial Terms, and Nieman Lab first reported on the change. The update was originally set to go into effect on October 30, but following backlash, Meta changed the effective date to November 20. Adding to the confusion, Meta then removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases, Nieman Lab reported, and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” where previously it said that data would be used for all Meta products. Those terms still allow Meta plenty of leeway for scraping users’ data to develop its products, however.

Several users based in the UK and EU have explained how to object on Instagram. On mobile: by clicking the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center, and clicking “object,” which goes to a form that asks users to write why they are objecting to their data being used. They received an email from Meta saying their objections were approved.

The New York Times has an antisocial aversion to linking: Another day, another the-New-York-Times-isn’t-linking controversy. The specifics here almost don’t matter because this happens seemingly every day, but basically the New York Times investigation about chemical plant polluters under the Trump administration was covered in much the same way by Hunterbrook, a news outlet fused with a hedge fund. The Times article—which led the Sunday print edition—uses similar photos, some of the same sources, and covers similar ground to Hunterbrook’s earlier investigation from February, with no acknowledgment or link whatsoever. After the cofounder of Hunterbrook rightfully ranted about this on X, the Times added an acknowledgment (but no link!!!) toward the bottom of the story. Puck’s Dylan Byers has a good rundown about what happened, which includes parts of a three-paragraph Times’ spokesperson statement explaining at length why they don’t think they have to link. This is extremely antisocial, deranged behavior and it’s ridiculous that the Times is still getting away with this. Bottom line: I’m sure the Times was already working on this story, what with their massive newsroom. Even so, they got beat, and they should link. Journalism awards need to stop looking the other way when big outlets do this. This has happened to us many times and it actually does matter for smaller outlets and links are free. Let’s try them!

93cd6552b0b383d5: TOKYO: The vice president of Japan's football association quit on Wednesday saying the "series of responses" to controversies surrounding the World Cup did not align with his personal values.

Takeshi Okada, who coached Japan at the World Cup in 1998 and again in 2010, stepped down a week after the head of Asian football said the region supported Gianni Infantino's bid for re-election as FIFA president.
Asian Football Confederation (AFC) president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa delivered the unequivocal backing at a meeting in Tokyo.

It came weeks after the AFC had joined football bodies in Europe and North America in condemning Infantino over his plan to open FIFA's premium competitions such as the World Cup to private investors.
Infantino has faced calls to quit and lost the support of some associations in his bid to be re-elected to a fourth and final term.
Okada, who is one of three Japan Football Association (JFA) vice presidents, said he was stepping down "entirely of my own volition."
"Throughout my career I have treasured the social value of sport based on my conviction that sport must be conducted with integrity," he said.

"However, with regard to the series of responses surrounding the recent FIFA World Cup, there is a significant gap between those responses and my own beliefs, and as a sportsman I cannot accept them."
Infantino, who apologised for the failed private investment project, has headed FIFA since 2016 and is running for re-election in March.
Two months ago the AFC and Sheikh Salman signalled they could turn on Infantino.
A joint letter with European body UEFA and CONCACAF, representing federations in North and Central America and the Caribbean, declared football "belongs to no individual."
Okada said his decision had been "reached after careful and repeated deliberation."
"Taking into account our relationship with the AFC and the impact on Japanese football, I do understand that there are practical reasons for aligning our stance with that of the AFC," he said. - AFP
8bb3ff430045312a: PETALING JAYA: Bersatu is expected to contest eight of the 28 seats in the Melaka state election, including four where it will possibly face Pakatan Harapan, amid speculation of possible cooperation between the two.

Bersatu president Muhyiddin Yassin is scheduled to announce the party's candidates tomorrow night.
The speculation over Bersatu's seat allocation comes amid possible cooperation between the party and PH.
On Saturday, PH announced its candidates for 21 seats. If this remains unchanged until nomination day, Bersatu will face PH in Kelebang, Gadek, Pengkalan Batu and Ayer Keroh.
However, the source described the prospect of the two sides contesting against each other as a “friendly clash”.
Contacted by FMT, Mohamad declined to comment on speculation that he would contest in Kelebang. “We'll wait for the announcement of the candidates,” he said.
